 <description>Sis stänger ungdomshemmet Vemyra i Sollefteå efter att myndigheten beslutat att inte överklaga kammarrättens dom. Enligt chefen på Vemyra har Kammarrätten utgått från situationen hösten 2025 och inte tagit hänsyn till förändringar i verksamheten. – Kammarrätten har inte varit här och kollat läget, hur saker och ting fungerar idag, säger Aron Sivaplan, institutionschef.</description>

      <description>Norwegian har teke kontakt med rundt 5000 kundar og bede dei sperre bankkorta sine etter at ein leverandør til nettsidene deira er utsett for datainnbrot, melder NTB.

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/israel-med-ny-offensiv-_-tre-drept-1.18084431</link>
      <description>Israels hær sier den har innledet en operasjon i Hamas-kontrollerte områder i Gaza
Israel har innledet en militæroperasjon i det sentrale Gaza vest for den såkalte gule linjen, som har skilt Hamas-kontrollerte og israelsk-kontrollerte områder siden våpenhvilen trådte i kraft i fjor. Det opplyser militæret til AFP.
Vitner sier at israelske stridsvogner rullet inn på hovedveien Salahudeen, vest for den såkalte gule linjen som markerer grensen for de to tredjedelene av Gazastripen som fortsatt er under israelsk kontroll.
Den såkalte gule linjen ble etablert etter våpenhvilen i oktober 2025 og skiller israelskkontrollerte og palestinske soner i Gazastripen. Israelske styrker har gradvis flyttet den gule linjen og utvidet området under direkte militær kontroll i Gaza.</description>

A Republican senator says a U.S. defence department’s memo that reportedly placed restrictions on co-operation with Canada applies to things such as participating in think-tank conferences, not military operations. 

Sen. Mike Rounds was responding to a Washington Post report on Friday that said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth penned the classified memo putting restrictions on military co-operation with Canada last week. The paper reportedly said it had not seen the memo and offered no detail on its contents. 

The senator said the memo does not affect any U.S. defence personnel in Canada today and does not impact the North American Aerospace Defence Command, North Atlantic Treaty Organization operations or the Five Eyes security alliance.

“It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance (defence department) objectives,” Rounds told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday.  “(U.S. defence officials) must request permission for Canadian think-tank events or social engagements. And it is OK to attend any 9/11 events.”

Rounds said he and a delegation of U.S. senators attending the Halifax conference had just attended a meeting with Canadian officials and shared the information with them. Defence Minister David McGuinty told reporters hours earlier he was unaware of the memo’s contents.

“After listening to this, (Canadian officials) said it sounds like it’s nothing new, nothing different than what they’ve been really practising under for the last year-and-a-half,” said the South Dakota senator. 

McGuinty said earlier in the day that it was “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries and assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing. 

“I’ve seen no evidence of (a change). I’ve checked with our top military folks, they’ve seen no evidence of change. We continue to co-operate. We continue to work together,” McGuinty told reporters.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a response to the story about the memo that the defence department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”

The statement, made late Friday, added that the department is prioritizing bilateral cooperation that strengthens the defence of the U.S. and “shared hemisphere” while also supporting Canada’s ability to meet NATO obligations. 

“This guidance does not impact defense intelligence cooperation, our binational NORAD command, or our cooperation through NATO,” Parnell said.

Several U.S. senators at the Halifax event acknowledged their country’s standing around the world has been impacted by the aggressive policies of U.S. President Donald Trump. 

Senator Tim Kaine, a Democrat, said the memo doesn’t help relations with Canada. He said he’s hopeful things will change when the new U.S. Congress takes office in January. Democrats took control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in this month’s midterm election.

“The tone is bad and it’s unnecessary,” said Kaine. “And we understand this actually goes back a ways and it is just the formalization of something that is now months and months old. I do think the new Congress is going to change the tone dramatically.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

The post U.S. senator says Hegseth memo does not change military co-operation with Canada appeared first on CHEK.

British Columbia’s official Opposition says the new Conservative cabinet is getting ready to tear down existing housing plans after eliminating the Ministry of Housing and Municipal Affairs as a separate office.

NDP interim leader Jennifer Whiteside says it is “deeply disappointing” to see the housing portfolio become part of the new Ministry of Local Government, Housing, Sport and Culture. 

She says the Conservatives’ decision appears to be the first step toward scrapping existing housing legislation.

The former B.C. labour minister says in a statement that housing affordability is a generational challenge and B.C. deserves a government that is “fighting to fix it, not one that abdicates its responsibility.” 

Premier Lorne Doerkson said at a news conference Friday that his government will be working with the federal government in “every way possible” to develop housing. 

He said that he committed himself to combining some of the ministries and the housing ministry is one of them.

Criticism also came from the B.C. Greens and their leader Emily Lowan.

Lowan said she is concerned about the signal that comes from combining the housing portfolio with others.

“British Columbians are struggling in an impossible affordability crisis, and in the worst housing crisis in a generation, this government has downgraded the housing portfolio, alongside labour,” she said.

Doerkson promised during and after the campaign to repeal key aspects of the provincial housing legislation introduced by the former NDP government of David Eby.

“We will return housing decisions to the people and the communities, who know their neighbourhoods so much better than Victoria,” he said during the inaugural meeting of the Conservative caucus after the election earlier this month.

Doerkson was referring to the repeal of Bill 44, which New Democrats considerer their signature piece of housing legislation.

The legislation legalized higher densities on single-lot properties in municipalities with populations above 5,000 people, but also came with housing targets, which local governments have criticized. 

The future of the legislation now falls within the responsibility of first-time legislator Cathie Ounsted, a former municipal councillor in Greater Victoria, who will head the new ministry following her appointment. 

Whiteside said in her statement that British Columbians also deserve a government that reflects B.C.’s diversity. 

“It is shocking that women make up just one-third of cabinet,” she said. “(For) the first time in three decades, B.C.’s Chinese-Canadian community, the province’s largest visible minority group with nearly 600,000 people, has no representation at the cabinet table.”

Amazon workers at a warehouse in B.C. are celebrating after winning their first union contract — not only in B.C., but also in Canada, and the first contract for Amazon workers across North America.

Unifor Local 114 said the new deal covers 800 workers at the Amazon YVR2 facility in Delta.

An independent arbitrator made this happen, according to Amazon and the union, after the terms of the binding collective agreement came through last Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.

Unifor says the new deal brings wages up to $29 per hour by the end of the three-year agreement. It includes severance protections of up to 18 weeks, an extra week of paid vacation for workers with 10 years of service, a Women’s Advocate, a grocery benefit, stat holiday scheduling based on seniority and improved employee benefits, including ergonomic protections to combat the physical demands of the job.

“Amazon told everyone a union contract would never happen, but workers proved them wrong,” said Unifor national president Lana Payne. “These workers stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away. Their courage won the day.”

Union representatives and workers say it’s taken a lot of work to reach the deal before any celebrations took place on Friday.

READ More: Amazon, workers ordered by B.C.’s labour board to reach deal via binding arbitration

In July 2025, the B.C. Labour Relations Board certified Unifor Local 114 as a union for Amazon workers after the retail giant hired extra workers to block the workers’ attempts to organize a union. On August 4, 2026, the Board ordered binding arbitration, ruling Amazon’s actions had interfered with reaching an agreement.

Amazon is challenging the decision

Amazon is challenging the decision, criticizing the B.C. Labour Relations Board, saying the deal was achieved through an unfair process.

In a statement, Amazon says “an outside arbitrator imposed a collective agreement on our associates at YVR2, our fulfillment center in Delta, British Columbia, without giving associates the chance to ratify or vote on it.”

“Our associates weren’t allowed to vote on whether to accept it, which has become an unfortunate pattern with the British Columbia Labour Relations Board,” it adds.

Unifor’s western regional director Gavin McGarrigle says, “These Amazon workers now have the binding union contract they deserve and we intend to support them and thousands more improving their lives, in BC and elsewhere.”

The agreement runs until November 13, 2029.

Whether this new deal will expand to cover Amazon workers in other regions of B.C., including Vancouver Island, remains uncertain. Though the union says workers at other Amazon sites can talk to a Unifor organizer in confidence at organizing@unifor.org.

The Public Health Agency of Canada has reported losing another $2 million in pharmaceuticals from the national emergency stockpile because of the mechanical failure of a freezer.

The figure is in the annual federal public accounts published earlier this fall, and comes after the agency had to write off $20 million in pharmaceuticals from the stockpile a year earlier after another freezer malfunction.

The agency says the second loss involved a small portion of a specific drug treatment for responding to a biological threat.

“A mechanical failure prevented a freezer from maintaining its required temperature, which led to a small portion of a stockpiled drug treatment being exposed to temperatures outside the required storage requirements,” said Health Canada spokesperson Hélène-Annie Lavoie. “The affected products had to be disposed of as a result.”

Lavoie said the agency immediately launched an internal investigation and identified the cause of the problem.

She said the incident did not compromise Canada’s ability to respond to that potential threat, since the stockpile still had another treatment.

The official said she could not disclose the lost drug inventory for national security reasons. She said sharing that information could “expose sensitive operational details about how Canada prepares for and responds to chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or other public health threats.”

The agency says it has put in place new measures to prevent a recurrence.

The Canadian Press reported last year that an open freezer door caused the loss of medication worth $20 million at the national emergency stockpile in December 2024.

While officials again would not say exactly what was destroyed or how much, the agency said at the time it affected one type of therapeutic drug as a result of temperature fluctuations “caused by several factors.”

The Office of the Auditor General issued a report on the emergency stockpile in October which said the agency had written off more than $331 million in expired or damaged medical supplies. A spokesperson for the office confirmed both the $20 million loss and the $2 million loss, from the malfunctioning freezers, were included in that figure.

The national stockpile is a network of warehouses across the country where the government stores medical supplies, vaccines and emergency response equipment.

First established during the Cold War, the stockpile was initially intended to respond to a nuclear emergency.

Since then, it has been adapted to respond to outbreaks of diseases — including SARS and COVID-19 — natural disasters like hurricanes and floods, bioterror attacks and other emergencies.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

The message at the Victoria Sexual Assault Centre (VSAC) hasn’t changed much over four decades: It’s not your fault, help is available, and healing is possible.

These two women at the VSAC are at opposite ends of the spectrum. CEO Ashley Dryburgh has been here about three months, while Karen Wickham, VSAC clinic and access coordinator, started shortly after it opened in 1993.

Starting with a staff of three back then, now there are 30 permanent employees, 20 auxiliary staff and a dedicated group of highly trained volunteers who are completely committed to giving survivors, all survivors, what they need

“Anyone of any gender can experience sexualized violence and I’m so proud that we are a trans-inclusive organization,” said Karen.

Recognizing that Indigenous women and girls are particularly vulnerable, they’ve established an Indigenous response network as well.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

VSAC offers crisis support, counselling, forensic exams and outreach services. Staff here do as little or as much as the survivor wants.

“They can sit down and do some beading or just sit and be comfortable for a while,” said Ashley. “If they are just wanting medications that are commonly given after a sex assault, that’s all we’ll do. If they want their big toe looked at and that’s it, that’s all we’re going to do.”

But VSAC can do so much more.

“It provides hope, it provides healing, we provide education and connection and it ultimately makes our entire community a better, safer place to be for everybody,” said Karen.

And there is joy here as well.

“You have to balance the darkness with the light, and there isn’t a single day that goes by here where I don’t hear laughter in the corridors, where we aren’t trying to uplift each other,” said Ashley.

When asked if she ever felt like leaving, Karen said, “No.”

“It makes me feel very honoured that someone has allowed me to assist them as they’re going through their journey,” she said.

What has been created here is thoughtful, comfortable and safe. And this is the message:

“It’s not your fault, there is help available and healing is possible,” said Ashley.

Whether in the clinic room with a handmade quilt, in the healing room, even in the hallways adorned with gifted art from survivors and staff alike, the Victoria Sexual Assault Centre is here, still, after 40 years, to care for those who need it.

There are many questions and few answers after a woman in critical condition arrived at the Port Hardy hospital after it had closed for the night.

“Frankly, it’s been very upsetting,” said Dr. Alex Nataros, a family physician with North Island Community Health Centre.

Thursday night, a woman arrived at the Port Hardy Hospital after 5 p.m., when the emergency room was closed.

Instead of being seen inside by doctors, she was treated in the parking lot by paramedics.

Eventually she made it inside the hospital where she couldn’t be resuscitated and was pronounced dead.

For nearly four years, the Port Hardy’s emergency room closes at 5 p.m. due to reported health provider shortages.

Nataros says a fellow North Island doctor was doing their rounds with patients in the 18-bed community hospital Thursday night after 5 p.m., when tragedy struck outside.

“My colleague is obviously very shaken up that this person died,” said Nataros.

Nataros says paramedics were performing CPR outside “for a prolonged period of time.”

“That is unusual,” said Nataros, who doesn’t know why the woman wasn’t taken to the nearest open hospital in Port McNeill.

BC Emergency Health Services (BC EHS) says at 5:11 p.m. Thursday, a paramedic at the hospital “became aware that there was a patient in need of medical treatment in the hospital parking lot.”

“Two additional ambulances responded to the scene. Paramedics provided emergency medical treatment to the patient, who was transferred to the care of Port Hardy Hospital staff in critical condition,” said BC EHS in a statement.

Island Health says it’s reviewing the circumstances of the case with BC EHS.

The BC Coroners Service says it’s also investigating the death.

Nataros was suspended by Island Health in 2023 from working in its emergency rooms following patient and healthcare worker complaints raising patient safety concerns.

He has also been outspoken in his criticism of Island Health over staffing shortages and advocacy for reopening Port Hardy Hospital’s overnight emergency services, and sees the death as related to Port Hardy’s ongoing nightly emergency room closures.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

“There’s been deaths, and too many deaths,” said Nataros. “It’s unacceptable. It’s reprehensible that our emergency has been closed for almost four years.

“I’m hopeful that the new Minister of Health Ryan Peterson, as well as our North Island MLA Anna Kindy in her new role as Minister of State for Rural Issues, will address this urgently and get Port Hardy emerge open as the primary emerge for the North Island.”

Peterson and Kindy were unable to comment Friday as they were only sworn into their new cabinet roles today, however, Kindy has previously been outspoken on the issue, as has B.C.’s Premier Lorne Doerkson.

“We will reverse ER closures and increase rural health care access,” promised Doerkson on October 5th, speaking outside 100 Mile House’s hospital.

“To support this, we will create a $50 million emergency fund which will be available for rural medical practices to prevent closures and aid recruitment.”

You might not know the name Terry Wilson, but if you’ve spent a lot of time in Fernwood, you know Terry the Bubble Man.

He was the guy in Fernwood Square in curious clothes, blowing massive bubbles into the air for, and occasionally at strangers. Whatever it took to get a smile.

And he did it for decades.

Terry the Bubble Man died recently at the age of 82, leaving a noticeable absence in a neighbourhood where he had become something of an institution.

The news prompted an outpouring of memories on Reddit, with people sharing stories of childhood encounters, chance conversations and the simple comfort of knowing Terry was around.

“He kinda dressed like a wizard,” said Victoria City Coun. Jeremy Caradonna at Wilson’s daily coffee stop, Little June.

For some, Terry was part of growing up in Fernwood.

Soli, who lived about a block away from the square, remembers chasing and popping hundreds of his bubbles as a kid.

“It was always nice to see him around, even if I wasn’t chatting with him, just kind of knowing he’s still there,” Soli said.

At Little June, staff knew Terry by name and his order by heart.

“Espresso. Terry always got an espresso,” said Jacqueline.

While thousands of people may have crossed paths with Terry over the years, not everyone knew much about the man behind the bubbles.

Graham Benesch did. The two were neighbours for 35 years, and Benesch says he last saw Terry just two days before his death.

He remembers a man who quietly looked out for the people around him.

When it snowed, Benesch says, Terry would sometimes shovel the walkway outside his building without anyone knowing who had done it.

“That man would go out of his way to help you. Without you even knowing,” Benesch said. “It’s a huge loss for Fernwood. A huge loss for Victoria.”

Terry’s outlook on life was captured in a 2013 Shaw TV interview, when he talked about the importance of holding onto a sense of childhood wonder.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

“It’s important not to let the kid part of us go as we get older,” Terry said.

It’s a sentiment that seems to have resonated with a lot of people in Fernwood.

Caradonna is bringing a motion to Victoria city council to explore a small memorial in Terry’s honour. Ideas include a plaque, a bench or perhaps some kind of permanent bubble installation.

Terry didn’t leave behind any known wishes for a memorial. But the neighbourhood he called home is already thinking about how to remember him.

For Benesch, the reason people connected with Terry was simple.

“He just wanted to see people smile.”

And for a man who spent so many years putting bubbles into the Fernwood sky, that’s not a bad legacy to leave behind.
